setting: A short lecture in an art history class about why Impressionist painters worked outdoors and how critics first responded.
narrator_intro: Listen to part of a talk in an art history class.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: In the 1870s, a group of French painters began working in a way that shocked many viewers.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Instead of finishing every detail in a studio, Impressionists often painted outdoors to catch changing light.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: They used short, visible brushstrokes and brighter colors placed side by side.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: From a distance, those strokes blend in the viewer’s eye; up close, the surface looks rough and unfinished.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Subjects were everyday scenes—cafés, train stations, rivers, and ordinary people—not only gods or kings.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Early critics mocked the style; the name “Impressionism” itself began as an insult after a painting titled Impression, Sunrise.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Dealers and independent exhibitions helped the artists reach buyers outside the official Salon.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Over time, the public grew used to the look, and museums later treated these works as modern classics.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: What matters for us is the shift: painting became about momentary perception, not only polished storytelling.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Next week we'll compare Impressionism with Post-Impressionist approaches by Seurat and Cézanne.

narrator_outro: Now get ready to answer the questions.

questions.narrator_text: What is the talk mainly about?

options.text: Why the Salon banned all landscape art forever
How Impressionist painters changed subject and technique in the 1870s
How digital cameras create modern museum photos
How to stretch a canvas for oil painting

questions.explanation: The professor explains outdoor light, brushstrokes, everyday subjects, and early criticism of Impressionism.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing C—the Salon is mentioned as an official path artists sometimes bypassed, not a total ban on landscapes.
questions.correctAnswer: How Impressionist painters changed subject and technique in the 1870s

questions.narrator_text: Why did many Impressionists paint outdoors?
questions.explanation: She says they often painted outdoors to catch changing light.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A or C—those reasons are not given.

questions.narrator_text: How did the name “Impressionism” begin, according to the professor?

options.text: As an insult from early critics after Impression, Sunrise
As a brand name invented by a paint company
As a title required by the Salon for every work

questions.explanation: The name began as an insult after a painting titled Impression, Sunrise.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—early response was mockery, not an award.
questions.correctAnswer: As an insult from early critics after Impression, Sunrise

questions.narrator_text: What shift in painting does the professor emphasize?

options.text: A requirement to finish every canvas indoors
A rule that artists must paint only kings and gods
A rejection of all color in favor of black and white
A move toward momentary perception rather than only polished storytelling

questions.explanation: She says painting became about momentary perception, not only polished storytelling.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing B—everyday scenes replaced a focus only on gods or kings.
questions.correctAnswer: A move toward momentary perception rather than only polished storytelling
